My coworkers and I were talking about New Horizon and its awesome accomplishment when one of them said "I image it would be tough to navigate that into place". I said I was under the impression it was preset before launch based on math and science and magic. So, how does New Horizon (and other space vehicles) navigate?
ELI5: How do space exploration vehicles, like New Horizon, navigate to their destination?

Math. Lots and lots of math. You have to calculate where you are in relation to your target, how fast it's going, where it's going to be when you get there, and what you might encounter along the way. This part is important because it can help you get there.

This is how we got to the comet recently. http://i.imgur.com/TUkKuhf.gif We took lots of energy from planets to position the probe perfectly with the comet.

If you want to see someone cheat at doing some of the math, the physics in Kerbal Space Program are pretty accurate, as far as orbital mechanics go. The computer is doing the calculations as you're setting the path, but the process is the same: Escape Earth's gravitational well in a way that sends you towards where your target will be in the future.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jiB2ywSM6i0

That gif was absolutely incredible. I was literally on the edge of my seat watching. It just blows my mind that a series of spectacular events like that has to happen in order to reach your goal. Regardless of the planning that goes into it, it is amazing. Thank you for that.

There is a lot of math involved but the actual math isn't very complicated. Isaac Newton could probably calculate it fairly easily if the data was presented to him in a way he could understand. It's not like you need to run super detailed computer simulations like they do for instance with weather or fluid simulations. The huge forces and time involved relative to the craft means there's not much point being too accurate as you can rather make tiny adjustments along the way.

It still blows my mind, it's incredibly impressive! Perhaps even more impressive once you realize the math involved was invented over 300 years ago.

EDIT: I realized one part of this which can require some truly staggering math actually. Finding the most optimum path and launch time given a set of parameters (overall time, energy required, launch site, intersect speed and angle, etc etc). This problem I can imagine absolutely needing some seriously complex number-crunching!

By a series of complex trajectories which are calculated well in advanced of the launch, though New Horizon does contain thrusters to make minor corrections to its trajectory as needed (you cannot predict everything after all).

In order to build up the velocity required to reach Pluto within our life-times, Horizon had to perform various manoeuvres all around the solar system, using the gravitation pushes it gained from each encounter with more massive bodies, such as Jupiter, to accelerate.

In order for something like this to be possible, we first had to solve the three body problem.

Basically, New Horizons sends signals to Earth that let us know where it is in our solar system. We use NASA's Deep Space Network to help track where the spacecraft is going. As the spacecraft gets closer to its destination, there are a series of opportunities for us to correct the trajectory using engine burns in order to accurately guide it towards the objective.

http://www.skyandtelescope.com/astronomy-news/new-horizons-navigating-to-pluto-040320154/

Simple: the New Horizons is about 3m in size, asteroids in the asteroid belt are about 1,000,000,000m apart and just a few of them are over 1000m wide... so it hopes not to be the 1/1,000,000,000,000 thing to hit any of them.

The course is plotted well in advance with the help of computer simulations. We can actually explore spacetime in our models, plotting exactly where everything will be at any instant in the future. We can find favorable launch windows when multiple planets/moons are arranged in beneficial ways and even inspire missions to make the most of such opportunities.

A lot of the difficulty in space travel is in the harshness of the environment; extremely hot and cold temperatures, unpredictable and powerful radiation bursts, and the possibility of hitting some piece of space debris at enormous speed, etc. Combine all these risks with the length of time that the craft needs to not break down for, often many years - even decades, and you see that incredibly detailed plans must be followed carefully over long periods of time.

Space exploration is incredibly difficult, but the knowledge we gain in return is exciting enough to be worth it.
